A real forecast: electricity demand, against the tidyverts

Source: vignettes/electricity-demand.Rmd
electricity-demand.Rmd

The other vignettes show the API. This one asks a harder question: is the foundation model actually any good?

We forecast Victorian daily electricity demand with TimesFM 2.5 and put it in the same mable as seasonal naive, ETS, and ARIMA, then score all four on held-out data with fabletools::accuracy(). Nothing here is special-cased for zukzeit — the foundation model is just another column.

Chunks are not evaluated when the vignette is built, because that would download a 925 MB checkpoint during R CMD check. Every output below was produced by running the code as written.

Why electricity demand

Time-series foundation models are pretrained on large corpora and then applied without task-specific training. TimesFM is a decoder-only transformer pretrained on roughly 100 billion time points, and its authors report zero-shot accuracy close to supervised models trained per dataset (Das et al. 2024). Chronos reports a similar pattern from a different architecture (Ansari et al. 2024).

Where that holds up varies a lot by data, and the benchmark literature is specific about it. GIFT-Eval evaluates across seven domains and a range of frequencies precisely because performance is not uniform (Aksu et al. 2024). Energy is one of the domains where these models tend to do well: daily and hourly load has strong, stable multi-scale seasonality and long history. Reviews of foundation models in power-system forecasting treat load as a leading application while being clear that classical methods remain competitive in places (Za’ter and Hodge 2026).

The other half of that literature matters just as much. Foundation models are not uniformly better — statistical baselines remain hard to beat at very high frequencies and on short histories, and benchmark work repeatedly recommends scoring against naive and seasonal-naive baselines before trusting a foundation model (Aksu et al. 2024). That is exactly what this vignette does, and it is why SNAIVE() is in the comparison rather than a formality.

So this is a favourable case, chosen deliberately. Run the same comparison on your own series before concluding anything about it.

The data

tsibbledata::vic_elec is half-hourly operational demand for Victoria, Australia, 2012–2014, from the Monash Time Series Forecasting Archive (Godahewa et al. 2021). We aggregate to daily totals in gigawatt-hours, which leaves a clean weekly cycle plus a strong annual temperature effect.

library(zukzeit)
library(tsibbledata)
library(tsibble)
library(fable)
library(dplyr)

daily <- vic_elec |>
  index_by(Date = as.Date(Time)) |>
  summarise(Demand = sum(Demand) / 1000) |>
  filter(Date >= as.Date("2012-01-01"))

daily
#> # A tsibble: 1,096 x 2 [1D]
#>   Date       Demand
#>   <date>      <dbl>
#> 1 2012-01-01   228.
#> 2 2012-01-02   275.
#> 3 2012-01-03   259.
#> # ℹ 1,093 more rows

Hold out the last 28 days:

h <- 28
train <- daily |> filter(Date <= max(Date) - h)
# 1,068 training days, 28 held out

Four models, one mable

TSFM() is a fabletools model definition, so it composes with everything else in the tidyverts. Note that only three of these four are fitted: TimesFM is zero-shot, so its “training” just binds the history for the key.

fits <- model(
  train,
  snaive  = SNAIVE(Demand ~ lag("week")),
  ets     = ETS(Demand),
  arima   = ARIMA(Demand),
  timesfm = TSFM(Demand,
                 model_id = "google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch",
                 device = "cpu")
)

fits
#> # A mable: 1 x 4
#>     snaive           ets                             arima         timesfm
#>    <model>       <model>                           <model>         <model>
#> 1 <SNAIVE> <ETS(M,Ad,M)> <ARIMA(0,0,1)(0,1,1)[7] w/ drift> <TSFM[timesfm]>

fabletools selected ETS(M,Ad,M) and ARIMA(0,0,1)(0,1,1)[7] w/ drift on its own — both picked up the weekly seasonality.

If arima comes back as <NULL model> with a warning, install urca: fable::ARIMA() needs it for unit-root tests, it is only suggested by fable, and fabletools::model() degrades a failed fit to a null model rather than erroring so that one bad column cannot discard the rest of the mable. That is usually the cause, not the data.

Forecasting and scoring is the ordinary tidyverts workflow:

fc <- forecast(fits, h = h)
accuracy(fc, daily) |> arrange(RMSE)
.model RMSE MAE MAPE MASE
timesfm 14.16 6.82 4.53 0.472
arima 29.18 17.41 10.92 1.203
ets 31.85 19.89 12.34 1.375
snaive 33.64 23.24 13.86 1.607

Zero-shot TimesFM roughly halves the error of the best fitted classical model on this window. Read MASE first: it scales error by the in-sample seasonal-naive benchmark, so below 1 is better than seasonal naive. TimesFM is at 0.47; ARIMA and ETS are both above 1, meaning that on these 28 days they did worse than the naive benchmark they were fitted to beat.

Two honest caveats. This is a single 28-day window, so treat it as one observation, not an estimate of expected performance — fabletools::stretch_tsibble() gives proper rolling-origin evaluation, and vignette("rolling-origin-tuning") shows that pattern. And the checkpoint was pretrained on a large corpus whose exact contents are not public, so contamination cannot be ruled out for a public benchmark dataset like this one.

Prediction intervals

The forecast carries predictive quantiles, not just a point:

tf <- fc |> filter(.model == "timesfm")
quantile(tf$Demand, 0.1)   #> 221.6 206.6 186.8 ...
quantile(tf$Demand, 0.5)   #> 230.4 214.8 194.0 ...
quantile(tf$Demand, 0.9)   #> 240.9 225.5 204.9 ...

hilo(tf, 60)
#> # A tsibble: 3 x 5 [1D]
#>   .model  Date            Demand .mean                  `60%`
#>   <chr>   <date>          <dist> <dbl>                 <hilo>
#> 1 timesfm 2014-12-04 quantile[3]  231. [223.7762, 238.2957]60
#> 2 timesfm 2014-12-05 quantile[3]  215. [208.6656, 222.8651]60
#> 3 timesfm 2014-12-06 quantile[3]  195. [188.6090, 202.1633]60

hilo(tf, 80) is the one to watch out for: it returns an NA lower bound. hilo() computes (1 - 80/100)/2, which in floating point is 0.09999999999999998 — about two ulps below 0.1. TimesFM’s lowest trained quantile is exactly 0.1, and distributional will not extrapolate past the outermost percentile it holds, so the lower bound comes back missing. Widening the request does not help, because the checkpoint emits only 0.1 through 0.9 and nothing outside. Use an interval that lands inside the trained grid, as above, or read the quantiles directly.

Where the point forecast lives

fabletools derives .mean from the distribution, so for a TSFM() fable it is the distribution’s mean. The engine’s own point forecast is the exactly evaluated median, which median() recovers on any route:

median(tf$Demand)

The plain-R and as_fable() routes report that median in .mean directly. The distributions are identical across routes; only the summary differs.

Scaling to a panel

fabletools evaluates one key at a time, so TSFM() runs the engine once per series. The checkpoint is loaded once and reused from the resident cache, but the forward passes are not batched. For a wide panel — aus_retail has 152 series — the batched route is much faster:

retail_fc <- forecast(
  zuk_pretrained("google/timesfm-2.5-200m-pytorch", device = "cpu"),
  aus_retail, h = 12,
  index = "Month", key = "Series ID", target = "Turnover"
)
nrow(retail_fc)                      #> 1824  (152 series x 12 months)
fabletools::as_fable(retail_fc)

All 152 series in one batched call takes about 10 seconds on CPU, including loading the checkpoint.

Use TSFM() when you want the model inside a mable next to other models, as above; use forecast() plus as_fable() when you want throughput.

What to take from this

On daily electricity demand — long history, strong seasonality, a domain the literature flags as favourable — a zero-shot foundation model beat three fitted classical models by a wide margin, with no tuning and no training.

That result is real but narrow. The same benchmark literature that reports strong zero-shot performance also reports that these models lose to simple baselines on short, noisy, or very high-frequency series. zukzeit is built so the comparison above is cheap to run: put TSFM() in the mable next to SNAIVE() and let accuracy() settle it on your data.

References

Aksu, Taha, Gerald Woo, Juncheng Liu, et al. 2024. “GIFT-Eval: A Benchmark for General Time Series Forecasting Model Evaluation.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2410.10393. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10393.

Das, Abhimanyu, Weihao Kong, Rajat Sen, and Yichen Zhou. 2024. “A Decoder-Only Foundation Model for Time-Series Forecasting.” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 235. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/das24c.html.
Godahewa, Rakshitha, Christoph Bergmeir, Geoffrey I. Webb, Rob J. Hyndman, and Pablo Montero-Manso. 2021. “Monash Time Series Forecasting Archive.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2105.06643. https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.06643.
